Do Black Hole Stars Exist
Black hole stars may have powered the universe’s first light.

Astrophysics postdoctoral fellow Rohan Naidu of MIT Kavli Institute for Astrophysics and Space Research, explores the idea that some early cosmic objects were not powered by nuclear fusion like our Sun, but by a black hole at their core. These massive, gas-filled structures could explain the mysterious “little red dots” spotted in deep space images of the early universe. If true, black hole stars may have played a major role in the rapid growth of supermassive black holes and the formation of the first galaxies.

How We Find Earth-Like Planets
Finding another Earth isn’t easy, it’s a cosmic challenge. 🌍

Avi Shporer, a research scientist at the MIT Kavli Institute, studies how astronomers detect planets beyond our solar system. We’ve found thousands of exoplanets, but Earth-sized, rocky worlds remain some of the hardest to spot. Their small size makes them incredibly difficult to detect around distant stars. Their year-long orbits make them even harder to find, which is why so few true Earth-like planets have been confirmed.

IC 1396 - The Elephant's Trunk Nebula (SHO, 23hrs)
Full-resolution image: [https://app.astrobin.com/i/u5q68q](https://app.astrobin.com/i/u5q68q)

Floating in Cepheus, roughly 2,400 light-years away, this is IC 1396, a vast emission nebula over 100 light-years across, ionised by the massive star system HD 206267 at its heart. Snaking through the glow is the Elephant's Trunk: a dense, dark pillar of gas and dust about 20 light-years long, where gravity is forming new stars even as radiation slowly erodes it away.

The whole region spans nearly 3° of sky, or about six full moons side by side. That faint blue "star" to the right isn't a star at all, but PK 100+04.1, a planetary nebula: the glowing shell ejected by a dying star, shining almost entirely in ionised oxygen.

Two more faint objects caught my eye in this frame: a blue, semi-circular cloud near the top, and a red, two-lobed shape to the left of the main nebula. I nearly submitted them as new discoveries, but both turned out to be known planetary nebulae, Cr 1 and StDr 4 (just obscure enough that I'd never crossed paths with them before).

The light in this image left IC 1396 around 374 BC. Back on Earth, Athens had just lost the Peloponnesian War, her Long Walls torn down after her last fleet was destroyed at the Hellespont; Socrates was condemned to death in Athens, while Hippocrates founded his school of medicine on Kos. All of that happened before this light even began its journey.

Open-source browser model of the universe built from HYG, Gaia, NED and JPL catalogs
There's a browser-based model of the universe at "Your Eyes In Space" that this sub might appreciate. Free, open source, nothing to install

It's basically real catalogs wired into one continuous scene: Solar System bodies on JPL elements with a time control, 109,000 stars from HYG with their parallaxes and spectral types, 55 galaxies at NED/SIMBAD distances, Sgr A\* with the S-stars on their GRAVITY/Keck orbits, a handful of other black holes and pulsars with catalog parameters, nebulae and clusters at literature positions, and the deep-space probes on their trajectories. Anything that isn't catalog data is labelled procedural, and there's a toggle that tints all of it so it's always clear what's real and what's filler.

The plan for it is to grow into a proper learning platform, basic physics and astrophysics with the universe as the blackboard. There are some narrated tours in there already as a first step. If something's in the wrong place or a distance doesn't match the literature, the project's on GitHub and takes issues.

Why does light take so long to escape a star? A random walk, from a 3D atmosphere to the blackboard
Apparently I keep coming back to this example... The hair, shirt and classroom change a bit with the years; the random walk remains. Consistency of a physics professor, perhaps? :-)



Here we go from a photon finding its way through our 3D model atmosphere to the simplest possible blackboard model: one step forwards, or one step backwards. The average displacement is zero, so that won’t get us very far. The mean square gives us something more useful.



The neat up-and-down argument is inspired by The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Volume I, §6–3, “The random walk”. Still my favourite way to get to that familiar square root of N.



Lectures and visualisations by Jon Sundqvist, Institute of Astronomy, KU Leuven. The stellar-atmosphere calculation is part of SUPERSTARS-3D.



A note on the two examples in the opening: the 9.7 million scatterings and roughly 98 minutes describe this particular path through our simulated hot-star atmosphere. The roughly 100,000-year solar diffusion timescale refers to a different problem and depends on the solar model.



Questions and corrections are welcome, as always. Enjoy :-)

Is the universe really flat?
This image shows the results of the BOOMERanG experiment, which studied the cosmic microwave background radiation, the remnant radiation from the Big Bang. The measurements showed that the universe is geometrically flat on a cosmological scale, meaning that the curvature of spacetime is very close to zero, rather than a two-dimensional surface. This finding is one of the most important discoveries in cosmology because it supports the Big Bang model and is consistent with the predictions of the theory of cosmic inflation, which posits that the massive expansion at the beginning of the universe resulted in its geometry appearing flat. The WMAP and Planck missions later confirmed this result with even greater precision, making the flat universe model the most consistent with observational evidence available to date.
